items.title: The local flow of an autonomous first-order system
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let U subset R^n be open and F:U->R^n continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable. For a in U let x(. ;a):I_a->U be the unique maximal solution of x'=F(x) with x(0)=a. The flow domain is Omega={(t,a):t in I_a}; the local flow is Phi:Omega->U, Phi(t,a)=x(t;a), and Phi_t is the time-t partial map. Phi_0(a)=a and the composition law are not part of the definition; they are proved separately.
items.strategy: Define the flow as the solution family of the autonomous field, with all domain conditions explicit; no uniqueness or completeness statement is smuggled into the definition.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 2.1 (autonomous systems) and Section 6.1 (the flow of a dynamical system), printed pages 17-19 and 190-192
J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.3 (maximal solutions) and Section 1.4 (continuous dependence), printed pages 22-30

items.title: The local flow is a partial one-parameter group: identity, composition and inverse-time laws
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For the local flow of a continuous, locally state-Lipschitz autonomous field: (1) Phi(0,a)=a; (2) if (s,a) and (t,Phi(s,a)) lie in Omega then (s+t,a) lies in Omega and Phi(s+t,a)=Phi(t,Phi(s,a)); (3) if (t,a) lies in Omega then (-t,Phi(t,a)) lies in Omega and Phi(-t,Phi(t,a))=a.
items.strategy: Glue translates of the maximal solution through a using uniqueness and maximality of solutions.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 6.1 (properties of the flow phi(t, x); the cocycle identity), printed pages 190-192
J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.3 (gluing of solutions on overlapping intervals), printed pages 22-28

items.title: Continuous and Lipschitz dependence on the initial condition on a Picard-Lindelof cylinder
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let F be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable on the open set U, and let a_0 in U, h,R>0 with closed ball B(a_0,R) in U, M and L the supremum of |F| and a state-Lipschitz constant on that ball, and 0<=rho<R with hM<=R-rho and Lh<1. Then every a in the closed ball B(a_0,rho) has exactly one solution x(.;a) on [-h,h] with graph in [-h,h]xB(a_0,R), and for all a,b and s,t in [-h,h]: |x(t;a)-x(t;b)|<=e^{L|t|}|a-b|; |x(t;a)-x(s;a)|<=M|t-s|; and |x(t;a)-x(s;b)|<=e^{Lh}|a-b|+M|t-s|, so the map (t,a)->x(t;a) is Lipschitz on the compact cylinder.
items.strategy: Construct the solutions on a common Picard-Lindelof cylinder and apply the Gronwall inequality to the Volterra integral equation solved by the difference of two solutions.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Lemma 2.7 (generalized Gronwall inequality) and Theorem 2.8 with estimate (2.43), printed pages 42-44

J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.4 (continuous dependence on the initial data), printed pages 32-36, and Appendix A.7 (Gronwall)

items.title: Smooth dependence of an autonomous flow on the initial condition, and the variational equation
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let F:U->R^n be C^1, a_0 in U, T,R>0 with closed ball B(a_0,R) in U, M and L the suprema of |F| and |DF| there, and 0<rho<R-MT. Then: (1) every maximal solution through a in the closed ball B(a_0,rho) is defined on [0,T] with values in B(a_0,rho+MT), depends Lipschitz-continuously on a, and the map (t,a)->x(t;a) is continuous on the compact cylinder; (2) the variational equation Y'=DF(x(t;a))Y, Y(0)=I has a unique solution Y_a on [0,T] and a->x(t;a) is differentiable with D_a x(t;a)h=Y_a(t)h; (3) (t,a)->Y_a(t) is continuous and (t,a)->x(t;a) is C^1 with the displayed partial derivatives.
items.strategy: Trap the solutions in a compact ball and extend them by compact continuation, estimate differences with Gronwall, then compare the difference quotients with the solution of the variational equation using the uniform derivative remainder on the compact ball.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 2.4: Theorem 2.10 (the solution is C^k in the initial condition and satisfies the first variational equation), printed pages 45-48
J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.4 (continuous dependence and the variational equation), printed pages 32-40

items.title: The flow domain of a C¹ autonomous field is open and the flow is C¹ on it
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: If F:U->R^n is of class C^1 on the open set U and Phi:Omega->U is its local flow, then Omega is open in R x U and Phi is of class C^1 on Omega with partial derivative in t equal to F(Phi(t,a)).
items.strategy: Cover the reference trajectory by finitely many Picard-Lindelof steps with radially shrinking balls, invoke the smooth-dependence theorem on each step, and assemble the C^1 pieces by the composition law.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 2.4 (Theorem 2.10: the solution map is C^k in the initial condition) and Section 6.1 (the flow domain), printed pages 45-48 and 190-192

J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.4 and Section 2.3 (dependence on initial data and differentiability), printed pages 32-40 and 76-82

items.title: A transversal return of a C¹ flow yields a local C¹ Poincaré map, with inverse given by the reversed crossing
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let F be C^1 with local flow Phi, (t_0,x_0) in Omega, x_1=Phi(t_0,x_0), and h a C^1 function transverse at both crossings (Dh(x_0)F(x_0) and Dh(x_1)F(x_1) nonzero, h(x_0)=h(x_1)=0) with Sigma=h^{-1}(0). Then there are open A containing x_0, B containing x_1 and C^1 return-time functions tau:A->R, sigma:B->R with tau(x_0)=sigma(x_1)=t_0 and unique zero-crossing property; P(x)=Phi(tau(x),x) maps A cap Sigma C^1-diffeomorphically onto B cap Sigma cap Q^{-1}(A), where Q(y)=Phi(-sigma(y),y), with Q(P(x))=x on A cap Sigma and P(Q(y))=y on B cap Sigma cap Q^{-1}(A).
items.strategy: Apply the implicit function theorem to (t,x)->h(Phi(t,x)) at the forward crossing and to (t,y)->h(Phi(-t,y)) at the reversed crossing, shrink the two neighbourhoods so that the compositions are defined, and verify the inverse identities by uniqueness of the crossing time.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 6.4, Lemma 6.9 and the Poincare map (6.25), printed pages 197-198
J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.4 and Chapter 2 (flow differentiability and section maps), printed pages 32-40 and 76-90

items.title: Finite-time tangent growth rates and Lyapunov exponents of a C¹ flow
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For a C^1 field F with local flow Phi, a point (t,x) in Omega with t>0 and u nonzero such that D_x Phi_t(x)u is nonzero, the finite-time tangent growth rate is r(t,x,u)=t^{-1} log(|D_x Phi_t(x)u|/|u|). If lim_{t->infinity} r(t,x,u) exists in R it is the Lyapunov exponent of (x,u); if the limit does not exist, no exponent is assigned, and no value +infinity or -infinity is named.
items.strategy: Define the rate and the exponent from the derivative of the time-t map, with the existence of the limit an explicit clause and no spectral or ergodic interpretation attached.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 9.1, formulas (9.3)-(9.6): exponential rates for the linearisation of a flow along a hyperbolic orbit
C. Ulcigrai, MATH36206/MATHM6206 Topological and Symbolic Dynamics, Section 2.3 (rates of divergence and sensitivity)

items.title: The bilateral two-symbol shift space, its metric, its shift map and its cylinder sets
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: X={0,1}^Z is the set of bi-infinite binary sequences; d(s,t)=sum_{k>=0}2^{-k}|s_k-t_k| + sum_{k>=1}2^{-k}|s_{-k}-t_{-k}| is a well-defined real number by comparison with the geometric series; the shift is sigma(s)_k=s_{k+1}; a cylinder [w]_{p,q} prescribes finitely many coordinates. No measure is introduced.
items.strategy: Define the symbol space, its metric expression, the shift and the cylinders; the metric axioms are proved in the companion lemma and are not part of the definition.

references.title: C. Ulcigrai, MATH36206/MATHM6206 Topological and Symbolic Dynamics (University of Bristol/Manchester), Section 2.6: the full bi-sided shift space Sigma_N, and Section 2.7: the metric d_rho and cylinders C_{-m,n}(a_{-m},...,a_n)

items.title: The bilateral shift metric is a metric, cylinders are its basic balls, and the shift space is sequentially compact
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For X={0,1}^Z with the metric expression d: (1) d is a metric; (2) B(s,2^{-m}) is contained in [s]_{F_m} and [s]_{F_m} is contained in the closed ball B(s,2^{1-m}), so cylinders are open and form a basis; (3) X is sequentially compact, by an explicit choice-free diagonal construction; (4) under the Axioms of Countable and Dependent Choice, X is compact.
items.strategy: Verify the metric axioms termwise, identify cylinders with balls up to a factor two, diagonalise a sequence of binary sequences by stabilising coordinate restrictions, and convert sequential compactness into compactness under the stated choice axioms.

references.title: C. Ulcigrai, MATH36206/MATHM6206 Topological and Symbolic Dynamics, Section 2.7: the metrics d_rho on Sigma_N, Lemmas 2.7.1-2.7.2 identifying cylinders with balls, and Lemma 2.7.3 (every open set contains a cylinder)
E. Glasner and B. Weiss, Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (Nonlinearity 6, 1993; updated author version), Section 2: subshifts of the two-symbol shift and their compactness

items.title: Topological mixing, dense periodic points, sensitive dependence, and the stated chaos list
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For a map f of a metric space: f is topologically mixing when for all nonempty open U,V there is N with f^n(U) cap V nonempty for all n>=N; periodic points are the fixed points of some iterate and are dense when every nonempty open set meets them; f is sensitive when there is delta>0 such that for every x and epsilon>0 there are y within epsilon of x and n>=1 with d(f^n x,f^n y)>=delta. f is chaotic in the stated sense when it is continuous, topologically mixing, has dense periodic points and is sensitive.
items.strategy: Record the three-property chaos package as a definition of the chosen list, with the uniform quantifiers explicit; no entropy or measure-theoretic mixing is asserted.

references.title: C. Ulcigrai, MATH36206/MATHM6206 Topological and Symbolic Dynamics, Definitions 2.2.2-2.2.4 and 2.3.4 (topological transitivity, minimality, mixing and sensitive dependence)

E. Glasner and B. Weiss, Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (Nonlinearity 6, 1993, 1067-1075; updated author version), Section 0: the three properties (transitivity, dense periodic points, sensitivity) used in one standard definition of a chaotic system

items.title: The bilateral two-symbol shift is continuous, topologically mixing, has dense periodic points and is sensitive; it is chaotic in the stated sense
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: The bilateral two-symbol shift sigma on X={0,1}^Z is continuous, topologically mixing, has dense periodic points, and is sensitive with constant 1; consequently it is chaotic in the stated sense.
items.strategy: Use cylinders as a basis: continuity from the metric estimate, mixing by prescribing the two blocks at disjoint index sets for all large n, periodic points by repeating a finite block, and sensitivity by flipping a coordinate in the future tail.

references.title: C. Ulcigrai, MATH36206/MATHM6206 Topological and Symbolic Dynamics, Section 2.6 (periodic points of Sigma_A: Corollary 2.6.1) and Section 2.7, Theorem 2.7.1 (topological Markov chains: aperiodic transition matrices give topologically mixing shifts)
E. Glasner and B. Weiss, Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (Nonlinearity 6, 1993; updated author version), Section 0 (sensitivity) and Section 2 (sensitivity of subshifts)

items.title: Scope of Poincaré recurrence for mechanical systems: finite invariant volume and complete return maps
items.design_state: completed-scope-remark; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: The recurrence content of this page is supplied by published items under their stated hypotheses: finite measure, a measure-preserving time map, and (for Hamiltonian flows) a finite-volume invariant region on which the time map and all iterates are defined. Finiteness, definedness of all iterates, and the almost-everywhere character are qualifications that cannot be dropped; infinite measure and unconfined phase space fail the hypothesis, and the shift example is not identified with any smooth mechanical return map.
items.strategy: Collect the published recurrence statements with their hypotheses and the explicit counterexample to the infinite-measure analogue; assert no identification of the symbolic example with a mechanical system.

references.title: M. Einsiedler and T. Ward, Ergodic Theory with a view towards Number Theory, first four chapters with appendices (LMS-EPSRC Summer School 2010), Chapter 2 (Poincare recurrence, Theorem 2.11 and Exercise 2.2.3, printed pages 21-23)
A. Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, Lecture 18 (Hamiltonian flow invariance of symplectic volume), p. 105

items.title: Exponential dichotomy for a hyperbolic endomorphism: invariant stable and unstable subspaces with exponential estimates
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, T an endomorphism, and suppose no complex eigenvalue of T has real part 0. Then V=E_s direct-sum E_u with T-invariant E_s,E_u and constants C>=1, c>0 such that |e^{tT}v|<=Ce^{-ct}|v| for v in E_s, t>=0; |e^{tT}v|<=Ce^{ct}|v| for v in E_u, t<=0; |e^{tT}v|>=C^{-1}e^{ct}|v| for v in E_u, t>=0; and E_s, E_u are exactly the sets of v with e^{tT}v->0 as t->+infinity and -infinity respectively. No diagonalisability is assumed.
items.strategy: Split the spectrum into the open left and right half-planes, build real invariant subspaces from coprime factors of the minimal polynomial via a Bezout identity, estimate each Jordan block by its exponential series with the polynomial factor, and characterise the subspaces by the exponential estimates.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 9.1, Theorems 9.1 and 9.2 and formulas (9.2), (9.4), (9.6), printed pages 253-254
F. Ramponi, Notes on Lyapunov's theorem, Section 3 (the Lyapunov equation and the exponential estimate P = integral of e^{A^T t} Q e^{A t})

items.title: An equilibrium whose linearisation has all eigenvalues in the open left half-plane is locally exponentially stable
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let F:U->R^n be C^1 with F(0)=0 and suppose every complex eigenvalue of A=DF(0) has negative real part. Then 0 is a locally exponentially stable equilibrium: there are delta>0, beta>=1, gamma>0 such that every solution with |z(0)|<delta is defined for all t>=0 and satisfies |z(t)|<=beta e^{-gamma t}|z(0)|; in particular 0 is Lyapunov stable and asymptotically stable.
items.strategy: Build the positive definite Lyapunov matrix Q from the integral of e^{tA^T}e^{tA}, verify A^TQ+QA=-I by differentiating the integrand, and show that V=z^TQz decreases exponentially on a small compact sublevel set that traps every nearby solution by compact continuation.

references.title: F. Ramponi, Notes on Lyapunov's theorem, Sections 2-4: the Lyapunov function V = x^T P x with P = integral of e^{A^T t} Q e^{A t}, and stability via linearisation

G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 6.6 (Liapunov's method) and Section 9.1, Theorem 9.1, printed pages 205-209 and 253-254

items.title: A hyperbolic equilibrium whose linearisation has an eigenvalue with positive real part is unstable
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let F:U->R^n be C^1 with F(0)=0, A=DF(0) having no purely imaginary eigenvalue and at least one eigenvalue with positive real part. Then 0 is not Lyapunov stable: there is epsilon_0>0 such that for every delta>0 there are z_0 with |z_0|<delta and t_1>0 with the maximal solution defined on [0,t_1] and |z(t_1)|=epsilon_0.
items.strategy: Use the indefinite form built from the unstable and stable Lyapunov matrices; it grows exponentially on a small ball along unstable data, and compact continuation forces arbitrarily small data to leave a fixed neighbourhood in finite time.

references.title: F. Ramponi, Notes on Lyapunov's theorem, Section 4 (instability when the linearisation has an eigenvalue with positive real part) and the counterexamples x' = -x^2, x' = x^2

G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 9.2 (stable and unstable manifolds of a hyperbolic fixed point), printed pages 255-262

items.title: The mechanical first-order field, Lagrangian and energy of a configuration-dependent kinetic metric in a chart
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let Omega be open, M:Omega->M_n(R) be a C^2 field of symmetric positive definite matrices, U:Omega->R be C^2. The kinetic energy, Lagrangian and energy are T=(1/2)v^T M(q)v, L=T-U, E=T+U; the mechanical field is G(q,v)=(v, M(q)^{-1}((1/2)grad_q(v^T M(q)v)-(D_qM(q)[v])v-grad U(q))) with D_qM(q)[v]=sum v_k partial_k M(q). A mechanical equilibrium is a critical point of U.
items.strategy: Define the chart model, its Lagrangian, energy and first-order field, with the inverse of the positive definite kinetic metric understood as a matrix inverse; record the equilibrium convention and nothing physical.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 8.6, formulas (8.76)-(8.78): the harmonic oscillator with mass matrix M and stiffness W and the decoupled system after the substitution (P,Q)=(VM^{1/2}p, VM^{-1/2}q)
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 2.6 (small oscillations and the normal-mode equations), printed pages 37-45

items.title: Energy is conserved along solutions of the mechanical system with a configuration-dependent kinetic metric
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For a C^2 kinetic metric field M and C^2 potential U, every C^2 solution q of M(q)q''=(1/2)grad_q(q'^T M(q)q')-(D_qM(q)[q'])q'-grad U(q) satisfies d/dt E(q,q')=0; the energy 1/2 q'^T M(q)q'+U(q) is constant along every solution.
items.strategy: Differentiate the kinetic energy using the product rule and the derivative of the matrix field along the curve, substitute the equation of motion, and cancel the two configuration-dependence terms.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 6.7, formula (6.47) and Theorem 6.16: the energy E = (1/2)v^T M v + U(q) as a constant of the motion
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 1.2.3 (energy conservation), printed pages 4-5

items.title: Positive definite symmetric matrices have positive definite square roots, and the congruence M^{-1/2} K M^{-1/2} preserves symmetry and positivity
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For a symmetric positive definite matrix M: M is invertible with symmetric positive definite inverse; there is a unique symmetric positive definite square root M^{1/2} with (M^{1/2})^2=M; M^{-1/2} is symmetric positive definite with (M^{-1/2})^2=M^{-1} and M^{-1/2}MM^{-1/2}=I; and for symmetric non-negative K the congruence S=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2} is symmetric non-negative, positive definite exactly when K is.
items.strategy: Transfer positivity to the associated operators, use the unique non-negative square root, verify the inverse and congruence identities by matrix algebra, and transport definiteness through the congruence.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 8.6, formula (8.77): the matrices M^{1/2}, M^{-1/2} and the symmetric matrix M^{-1/2}WM^{-1/2}
Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition, Chapter 7 (positive operators and their square roots)

items.title: A C² local minimum has vanishing gradient and positive semidefinite Hessian
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: If U:Omega->R is C^2 and q_0 is a local minimum of U, then the gradient vanishes at q_0 and the Hessian is positive semidefinite: h^T D^2U(q_0) h>=0 for all h.
items.strategy: Apply Fermat's theorem along the lines t->q_0+th for the vanishing gradient, and the second-order Taylor expansion with the Peano remainder for the semidefiniteness; no strictness is assumed.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 6.7 (fixed points correspond to extremal points of the potential U), printed page 204
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 2.6 (equilibria and the second-order Taylor expansion of the potential), printed pages 37-40

items.title: Decoupling of the constant-coefficient quadratic system $Mq''+Kq=0$ into normal modes, with the zero-mode and energy identities
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let M be symmetric positive definite and K symmetric non-negative, and let O diagonalise S=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2} with eigenvalues lambda_i>=0. With z=O^T M^{1/2}q, q solves Mq''+Kq=0 iff z_i''+lambda_i z_i=0 for every i; each scalar equation with prescribed data has the complete solution a_i cos(omega_i t)+b_i sin(omega_i t) for lambda_i>0 (omega_i=sqrt(lambda_i)) and a_i+b_i t for lambda_i=0; the correspondence of initial data with the coefficients is a bijection; and the modal energies and 1/2 q'^T M q'+1/2 q^T K q are constant and sum to the total energy.
items.strategy: Transform the system by M^{-1/2} and the orthogonal diagonalisation of S, solve the decoupled scalar equations with a uniqueness argument, and verify the modal-energy identities by direct differentiation.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 8.6, formulas (8.76)-(8.79): decoupling M q'' + W q = 0 by V M^{-1/2} W M^{-1/2} and the mode energies
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 2.6 (normal modes and the mode frequencies), printed pages 40-45

items.title: A strict local minimum of the potential gives a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of the mechanical system, by energy conservation
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: Let M be a C^2 field of symmetric positive definite matrices, U be C^2 and q_0 a strict local minimum of U with grad U(q_0)=0. Then (q_0,0) is a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of the mechanical system: for every admissible epsilon>0 there is delta>0 such that every solution with |(q(0),v(0))-(q_0,0)|<delta is defined for all t>=0 and stays within epsilon. No asymptotic stability is asserted.
items.strategy: Use exact energy conservation: E-E_0 has a positive minimum on the sphere of radius epsilon, continuity of E gives a delta, and the energy barrier forbids a first exit; compact continuation then gives forward existence for all time.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 6.7, Theorem 6.16: a fixed point of Newton's equation is stable if the potential has a local minimum there
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 2.6 (stability of equilibria from the potential), printed pages 37-39

items.title: Linearisation of the mechanical system at an equilibrium: M(q_0) xi'' + D²U(q_0) xi = 0, and the small-oscillation quadratic model
items.design_state: completed-local-argument; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: At a mechanical equilibrium q_0 the mechanical field is totally differentiable with DG(q_0,0)(dq,dv)=(dv, -M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)dq); the linearised equation is xi''=-M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)xi, equivalently M(q_0)xi''+D^2U(q_0)xi=0, with M(q_0) symmetric positive definite and D^2U(q_0) symmetric. If q_0 is a strict local minimum then K=D^2U(q_0) is non-negative and the quadratic-mode theorem applies to the linearisation; the replacement of the nonlinear system by the linearisation is an approximation whose error is not estimated here.
items.strategy: Differentiate the explicit components of the field at the equilibrium, using that the v-dependent terms are quadratic in v and that the gradient of U vanishes, and identify the Hessian of U as the stiffness; restrict the quadratic-mode theorem to the strict-minimum case.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 8.6, formulas (8.76)-(8.77): linearisation of the potential at a critical point, M q'' + W q = 0 with W the Hessian
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 2.6, equations (2.113)-(2.116): expansion of the equation of motion about an equilibrium

items.title: Scope of the quadratic-mode and energy-stability results: exact quadratic model versus linearisation approximation
items.design_state: completed-scope-remark; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: The quadratic-mode theorem is an exact theorem about the constant-coefficient linear system with symmetric positive definite mass and symmetric non-negative stiffness; the linearisation proposition computes the exact first-order Taylor model at an equilibrium, and replacing the nonlinear system by it is an approximation whose error over a time interval is not estimated; the energy-stability theorem is an exact Lyapunov-stability statement for the nonlinear system at a strict minimum and asserts no attraction.
items.strategy: Separate the exact quadratic model, the linearisation approximation and the nonlinear stability theorem, and state explicitly which conclusions are and are not drawn in each case.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 2.6 (the small-oscillation approximation and its higher-order terms), printed pages 37-45

G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 6.7 (stability and non-asymptotic character of conservative equilibria), printed pages 203-205

items.title: The flow and variational equation of a linear system: Phi(t,a)=e^{tA}a
items.design_state: completed-local-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For the linear field F(x)=Ax: the flow is Phi(t,a)=e^{tA}a with Omega=R x R^n; the composition law is the exponential law e^{(s+t)A}=e^{sA}e^{tA}; D_a Phi(t,a)=e^{tA}; and the variational equation Y'=AY, Y(0)=I has the unique solution Y(t)=e^{tA} on every compact interval.
items.strategy: Verify the explicit exponential solution, its maximality, the flow identities and the variational equation directly from the exponential-series calculus.

items.title: Two coupled equal masses: mode frequencies sqrt(k/m) and sqrt((k+2c)/m), and the free zero mode when k=0
items.design_state: completed-local-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For m>0, k>=0, c>=0, the system with M=diag(m,m) and K=[[k+c,-c],[-c,k+c]] has S=K/m with eigenvalues k/m along (1,1)/sqrt 2 and (k+2c)/m along (1,-1)/sqrt 2. If k>0 the first mode oscillates with frequency sqrt(k/m), while if k=0 it is the free affine mode a_1+b_1 t along the centre-of-mass direction; the second mode oscillates with frequency sqrt((k+2c)/m) whenever k+2c>0, and both modes are affine if k=c=0. A zero eigenvalue is not an oscillator.
items.strategy: Multiply the explicit matrices, read off the orthonormal eigenvectors, and specialise the quadratic-mode theorem to each sign case of the eigenvalues.

items.title: The Poincaré return map of the planar isotropic oscillator on the line y=0 is the reflection x->-x
items.design_state: completed-local-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For F(x,y)=(y,-omega^2 x) and the section y=0 with reference point (1,0), the transversality conditions hold and the local Poincaré map is the reflection P(x,0)=(-x,0), with inverse Q(y,0)=(-y,0) and return time pi/omega on the section.
items.strategy: Write the explicit solution of the oscillator, identify the crossings of the section, and realise the local return map computed by the proposition on the section.

items.title: A non-hyperbolic equilibrium with no positive eigenvalue can still be unstable: x'=x^3
items.design_state: completed-local-counterexample; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: The statement that a C^1 field with F(0)=0 and no eigenvalue of DF(0) of positive real part has a Lyapunov stable equilibrium at 0 is false: for F(x)=x^3 the solution through x_0>0 blows up at t=1/(2x_0^2), so 0 is not Lyapunov stable although DF(0)=0 has real part 0 and no positive-real-part eigenvalue.
items.strategy: Exhibit the explicit blowing-up solution through every small positive initial value and refute the stability clause for every delta.

references.title: F. Ramponi, Notes on Lyapunov's theorem, final page: the counterexamples x' = -x^2 and x' = x^2 with linearisation zero, showing that stability cannot be decided from the linearisation when eigenvalues have zero real part
